title: ADHD Applications
subtitle: Evidence is protocol-, comparator- and outcome-dependent
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating adhd applications within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain adhd applications without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in adhd applications.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to adhd applications.

sections.explainSimply: Neurofeedback has been studied as a training approach for ADHD symptoms, especially attention and self-regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Earlier meta-analyses reported benefits, but rigorous blinded outcomes and recent syntheses have produced less favourable conclusions at group level.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Discuss evidence uncertainty, standard treatments, burden, cost and the difference between proximal ratings and blinded outcomes. Do not replace indicated care without shared decision-making.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand adhd applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A child improving during a long treatment course does not prove neurofeedback caused the change.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using adhd applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A child improving during a long treatment course does not prove neurofeedback caused the change. Evidence classification: mixed; recent high-quality synthesis does not show meaningful group-level benefit.
